title: The traditional method
subtitle: Champagne's way
objectives: Put the steps of the traditional method in order

steps.title: The steps
steps.body: A dry base wine is blended, then bottled with sugar and yeast, the liqueur de tirage. The bottle is sealed with a crown cap. A second fermentation raises alcohol by about 1.2 to 1.5% and makes carbon dioxide. The wine then rests on its lees, from 15 months for non-vintage Champagne to many years for top wines.
steps.highlight: Tirage, second fermentation, ageing on lees

steps.title: Getting the yeast out
steps.body: Riddling, or remuage, slowly turns and tilts the bottles until the dead yeast slides into the neck. It once took weeks by hand; machines called gyropalettes now do it in about a week. The neck is frozen and the cap removed: pressure pushes out the plug of ice and yeast. This is disgorgement. Then sweetened wine, the dosage, is added.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of the traditional method in order.
items: Add sugar and yeast, and seal
steps.explanation: The order ensures the yeast does its work, adds flavour, and is then removed cleanly.

steps.title: Dosage
steps.body: Dosage is a mix of wine and sugar added after disgorgement. It balances the high acidity of the base wine and decides the final sweetness: most Champagne is Brut, with up to 12 g/l. Brut Nature has none added. The traditional method is used for Champagne, Cava, Crémant, Franciacorta and many others.

options: Removing the frozen plug of yeast from the neck
steps.explanation: Disgorgement removes the yeast sediment, using the wine's own pressure to push out a frozen plug.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The second fermentation happens in the bottle you buy
Riddling moves the yeast to the neck; disgorgement removes it
Dosage balances acidity and sets the sweetness
